item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q025_classification_as_evolutionary_hypothesis","answer":"Assign it to a new superfamily within the existing fold, provided the match includes the fold’s defining core topology and arrangement rather than merely superficial shape. In SCOPe release 2.08, the hierarchy is class > fold > superfamily > family. A new family under an existing superfamily would assert probable common ancestry with that superfamily and a comparatively close relationship within it; the stated lack of convincing ancestry makes that claim unsupported. A new superfamily in the existing fold records the shared fold while declining to claim homology with existing superfamilies; adding future domains to this new superfamily would assert probable common ancestry among those members. A new fold would claim that no existing fold adequately captures the domain’s core topology and architecture, so it is appropriate only if the apparent resemblance fails detailed structural comparison. Class placement conveys only broad structural character, not common ancestry. Evidence for upgrading an evolutionary claim should combine sequence evidence with detailed conservation of the structural core, unusual shared features, and mechanistic or literature evidence—not fold similarity alone. Function must not be transferred solely from the fold; even superfamily-level transfer requires checking active-site residues and biological context, and family-level transfer is stronger but not automatic. An existing-fold structure may serve as a coarse modeling template, but fold membership alone does not justify homology, active-site, loop, or ligand predictions. Representative selection should favor a complete, correctly bounded, high-quality domain and should not imply that one representative captures the new group’s eventual sequence, structural, or functional diversity.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge","/api/v1/","/api/v1/levels"]}]}
